bibl.title: Priming words with pictures: Neural correlates of semantic associations in a cross‐modal priming task using fMRI

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our results indicate that cross‐modal and unimodal processing share a common neural network within the bilateral fronto‐temporal cortex.

span.label: cross-modal semantic priming (picture-word)
span.quote: The aim of the current study was to investigate between‐ (picture–word) and within‐modality (word–word) neural processing using semantic priming.

span.label: fmri
span.quote: The present study examined the neural correlates of uni‐ and cross‐modal priming using fMRI with a word–word and picture–word semantic priming task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Presentation of a prime activates its concept, and that activation spreads automatically along associative pathways in the semantic network to related concepts, so the related target is already pre-activated when it appears.
span.quote: The priming effect is explained by an automatic “spread of activation” between related word representations within the semantic network that occurs at short stimulus onset asynchrony [SOA < 400 ms; see Neely, 1991 for a review].

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The haemodynamic decrease for related pairs arises because pre-activation lowers the demand on semantic memory retrieval and selection, so less neural work is needed than for unrelated pairs.
span.quote: Hence, the response suppression is caused by reduced demands for the semantic memory retrieval or is the result of selection caused by the automatic spread of activation [Matsumoto et al., 2005 ; Tivarus et al., 2006 ].

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The shared right fronto-temporal deactivation is attributed to the easier semantic processing of associatively related concepts, an ease that does not depend on which modality delivered the prime.
span.quote: we assume that the deactivation of the right fronto‐temporal regions for related pairs reflects the ease of semantic processing for associatively related concepts that is independent of modality

span.label: The sample was restricted to male subjects, so gender effects on the reported lateralisation and language processing are untested here.
span.quote: We restricted our sample to male subjects due to the ongoing debate about gender specific effects for almost all types of cognitive demands, including language processing and lateralization [Baxter et al., 2003 ; Bermeitinger et al., 2008 ; Laws, 1999 ; Lloyd‐Jones and Humphreys, 1997 ].

span.label: Only artifact (man-made object) concepts were used, so the findings may not extend to natural/living concepts or to manipulable versus non-manipulable relations.
span.quote: In the current study, we used only artifacts to investigate the influence of different visual modalities on the processing of semantic associations.

span.label: a PRE-TEST established that the word pairs really were strongly related
span.note: eliminates: that a null or weak priming effect is a failure of the materials rather than of the hypothesis
span.quote: To ensure that the word‐pairs had a strong relationship a pre‐test was conducted.

span.label: four pseudo-randomised versions of the experiment counterbalanced across subjects
span.note: eliminates: that the conditions systematically influence one another through their order
span.quote: Four pseudo randomized versions of the experiment were counterbalanced across subjects to avoid a systematic effect of conditions on each other.

span.label: semantic priming
span.quote: In behavioral studies of semantic processing, a widely applied technique is automatic semantic priming using short SOAs. A task commonly used is the lexical decision task

span.label: cross‐modal
span.quote: Cross‐modal priming led to response suppression within the right inferior frontal gyrus. Common areas of deactivation for both modalities were found in bilateral fronto‐tempo‐parietal regions

span.label: response suppression
span.quote: Thus, response suppression is a special form of BOLD response “deactivation”, response enhancement a special form of BOLD

span.label: lexical decision
span.quote: A task commonly used is the lexical decision task. Generally, a prime word (e.g., frame ) is presented on a computer screen, followed by a string of letters (target) which can be a real word

span.label: unimodal
span.quote: Behavioral data revealed a priming effect for cross‐modal and unimodal word‐pairs. On a neural level, the unimodal condition revealed response suppression in bilateral fronto‐parietal regions

span.label: A NULL WHERE THE DESIGN EXPECTED A DIFFERENCE: `The comparison of both modalities revealed NO DIFFERENCES between uni‐ and cross‐modal semantic priming.` A picture priming a word behaves like a word priming a word. Set beside Chen2018, tagged earlier tonight - which separated two cross-modal primes by their time courses - this says the modality BOUNDARY itself costs nothing, while what crosses it still can
span.quote: The comparison of both modalities revealed no differences between uni‐ and cross‐modal semantic priming. In contrast, common regions of deactivation were found within bilateral fronto‐tempo‐parietal regions. The extensive involvement of the right‐lateralized fronto‐temporal clusters during semantic processing has been demonstrated in some studies. One hypothesis suggests, that the right frontal and temporal lobe maintains weak, diffuse semantic activations within a broader semantic field [Beeman and Chiarello, 1998 ; Jung‐Beeman, 2005 ; Raposo et al., 2006 ; Rossell et al., 2001 ]. For example, activation was found for distant semantic relations of words [Beeman et al., 1994 ], extraction of overall meaning from sentences [Kircher et al., 2001 ] and for related words that do not share many semantic features [Chiarello, 1998 ]. In addition, activation of the MTG bilaterally were found for semantic category judgments, i.e., the temporal lobe plays a critical role during semantic processing [Pugh et al., 1996 ]. For our results, we assume that the deactivation of the right fronto‐temporal regions for related pairs reflects the ease of semantic processing for associatively related concepts that is independent of modality. Support comes from several studies investigating semantic priming in the left and right hemisphere

span.label: THE SHORT SOA IS A CONTROL AND THE ALTERNATIVE IS NAMED: `In order to avoid STRATEGIC INFLUENCE OR EXPECTANCY which can affect priming‐specific patterns of activation ... we wanted to use fast, automatic, implicit processing, i.e., semantic priming with an short stimulus onset asynchrony.` The SOA is not a parameter, it is a fence - it makes strategy impossible rather than unlikely. Eighth record this sitting where a time course is load-bearing, and the first where it is used as a CONTROL rather than reported as a result
span.quote: In order to avoid strategic influence or expectancy which can affect priming‐specific patterns of activation [Grossman et al., 2006 ], we wanted to use fast, automatic, implicit processing

span.label: `response suppression` DEFINED BY SCOPE rather than by mechanism: it is `a special form of BOLD response deactivation, response enhancement a special form of BOLD activation IN THE CONTEXT OF SEMANTIC PRIMING EXPERIMENTS IN AN fMRI SETTING`. The definition carries its own boundary - the same neural word means this only here - which is exactly the move this corpus exists to record
span.quote: Thus, response suppression is a special form of BOLD response “deactivation”, response enhancement a special form of BOLD “activation in the context of semantic priming experiments in an fMRI setting

span.label: A SAMPLING DECISION WITH ITS REASON, AND ITS COST: `To minimize the variance and increase homogeneity within our sample, ONLY MALE SUBJECTS WERE MEASURED.` The rationale is stated and is statistical rather than theoretical - homogeneity bought at the price of generalising to half the population. Worth a row because the trade is made explicit rather than left to be noticed by a reader
span.quote: To minimize the variance and increase homogeneity within our sample, only male subjects were measured. Three experimental conditions were compared while brain activation was measured with a 3 T fMRI scanner

span.label: builds-on → Caramazza et al. [1990] (Organized Unitary Conceptual Hypothesis)
span.quote: Thus, our data support an amodal semantic system based on the hypothesis of Caramazza et al. [ 1990 ] rather than the hypothesis of multiple semantic systems [e.g., Paivio, 1991 ].

span.label: contradicts → Paivio, 1991 (multiple semantic systems)
span.quote: Thus, our data support an amodal semantic system based on the hypothesis of Caramazza et al. [ 1990 ] rather than the hypothesis of multiple semantic systems [e.g., Paivio, 1991 ].

span.label: replicates → Caramazza et al., 1990; Vandenberghe et al., 1996
span.quote: First of all, similar to other studies we found no difference between cross‐modal and unimodal priming on a behavioral or neural level [Caramazza et al., 1990 ; Vandenberghe et al., 1996 ].

span.label: cross‐modal —distinct-from→ unimodal
span.note: differs in: WHERE IN THE BRAIN, NOT HOW MUCH - both produce a behavioural priming effect and the comparison of the two revealed NO behavioural difference, while the neural suppression sits in bilateral fronto-parietal regions for unimodal and in the right inferior frontal gyrus for cross-modal · strength of the relation: 0.85 — Weighted 0.85 rather than higher because the distinction is NEUROANATOMICAL ONLY - behaviourally the paper reports no difference at all, and an edge read without that qualifier would overstate the separation. The null has its own sense row.
span.quote: Behavioral data revealed a priming effect for cross‐modal and unimodal word‐pairs. On a neural level, the unimodal condition revealed response suppression in bilateral fronto‐parietal regions

span.label: cross‐modal —operationalised-as→ response suppression
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — The neural effect is a DEACTIVATION - less BOLD signal for related than for unrelated pairs - so the priming benefit shows up as the brain doing less. Recorded because the sign is counterintuitive and a reader meeting `suppression` in a priming context needs it.
span.quote: Cross‐modal priming led to response suppression within the right inferior frontal gyrus. Common areas of deactivation for both modalities were found in bilateral fronto‐tempo‐parietal regions

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: The results of the ANOVA indicated that there was no main effect of modality ( F (1, 15) = 0.06, P = 0.81), but that subjects were faster in the related compared to the unrelated condition ( F (1, 15) = 14.73, P < 0.005).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The results represent the P values of the paired‐sample t ‐tests.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Sixteen healthy male subjects with an average age of 26.0 years (S.D. = 3.4) were recruited from the staff of the RWTH University Hospital Aachen and were paid a fee for participation.

span.label: outlier trimming by standard deviations
span.quote: Raw reaction time data were trimmed by eliminating responses exceeding the mean of every condition by more than two standard deviations to reduce skew [3.9%; Ratcliff, 1993 ].

span.label: Monte Carlo simulation
span.quote: we chose to employ Monte‐Carlo simulation of the brain volume to establish an appropriate voxel contiguity threshold [Slotnick et al., 2003 ].

span.label: maximum likelihood estimation
span.quote: The model parameters were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (ReML).

span.label: multiple comparison correction / type I error rate
span.term: multiple comparison correction / type I error rate
span.quote: Assuming an individual voxel type I error of P < 0.00005, a cluster extent of 4 contiguous resampled voxels was indicated as necessary to correct for multiple voxel comparisons at P < 0.05.

span.label: A significant behavioural priming effect was obtained in both the picture-word and the word-word conditions.
span.quote: In both modalities, subjects were faster in the related compared to the unrelated condition (cross‐modal condition: t (15) = 2.92, P < 0.01; unimodal condition: t (15) = 2.66, P < 0.05).

span.label: The size of the cross-modal priming effect was statistically indistinguishable from the unimodal one.
span.quote: A further t ‐test of priming effect sizes in cross‐modal and unimodal conditions revealed that the picture–word priming effect did not differ from the word–word priming effect ( t (15) = −0.45, P = 0.66

span.label: Unimodal word-word priming produced response suppression across bilateral fronto-parietal cortex.
span.quote: Subtraction of the unimodal related from the unimodal unrelated trials (unrelated > related; excl. masked with unimodal word‐nonword) revealed bilateral fronto‐parietal clusters of activation

span.label: Cross-modal picture-word priming produced response suppression confined to the right inferior frontal gyrus.
span.quote: The contrast cross‐modal unrelated > cross‐modal related (excl. masked with cross‐modal picture‐nonword) revealed activation in the right IFG.

span.label: The direct contrast between the two modalities yielded no significant modality-specific clusters.
span.quote: The comparison of both modalities revealed no differences between uni‐ and cross‐modal semantic priming.

span.label: Because the two modalities shared a common bilateral fronto-tempo-parietal deactivation network and differed nowhere, the data favour a single amodal semantic system over multiple modality-specific semantic systems.
span.quote: Thus, our data support an amodal semantic system based on the hypothesis of Caramazza et al. [ 1990 ] rather than the hypothesis of multiple semantic systems [e.g., Paivio, 1991 ].

span.label: priming effect
span.quote: The main outcome is the priming effect, i.e., subjects respond faster to the target if it was preceded by a related prime word (e.g., frame–picture ), compared to when it is preceded by an unrelated word (e.g., frame–stone ).

span.label: response suppression
span.quote: Response suppression is thought to reflect the attenuation of hemodynamic activity as consequence of priming, i.e., it reflects faster or “more efficient” processing of primed stimuli [Henson, 2003 ].

span.label: response enhancement
span.quote: Response enhancement is thought to be a correlate of cognitive processes that index the spread of activation itself [Henson, 2003 ; Marinkovic et al., 2003 ].

span.label: association (as used for the prime-target relation)
span.term: association (as used for the prime-target relation)
span.quote: Associations were defined as “external or complementary relations among objects” [Lin and Murphy, 2001 ] that shared functional (e.g., chalk–blackboard ) or part‐whole links (e.g., ladder–rung ).

span.label: Organized Unitary Conceptual Hypothesis (OUCH) / single amodal semantic system
span.term: Organized Unitary Conceptual Hypothesis (OUCH) / single amodal semantic system
span.quote: The second general model suggests a single amodal semantic system which is incorporated in the Organized Unitary Conceptual Hypothesis [OUCH; Caramazza et al., 1990 ].

span.label: automatic (versus controlled) processing, operationalised by SOA
span.term: automatic (versus controlled) processing, operationalised by SOA
span.quote: According to Neely [ 1991 ] automatic processing occurs if the SOA is under 400 ms. Therefore, we used an SOA of 350 ms.

span.label: modality (cross-modal picture-word vs unimodal word-word)
span.quote: Trimmed data were entered into a repeated measure ANOVA with modality (cross‐modal and unimodal) and relation (related and unrelated) as independent variables.

span.label: relation (related vs unrelated prime-target pair)
span.quote: Trimmed data were entered into a repeated measure ANOVA with modality (cross‐modal and unimodal) and relation (related and unrelated) as independent variables.

span.label: reaction time in the lexical decision task
span.term: reaction time in the lexical decision task
span.quote: Reaction time was measured from the moment the target was presented until the subject made a correct response.

span.label: error rate (percentage of incorrect lexical decisions)
span.term: error rate (percentage of incorrect lexical decisions)
span.quote: The percentage of errors was entered into a repeated measure ANOVA with modality and relation as independent variables.

span.label: lexical frequency, word length and relationship type of the stimuli (matched)
span.term: lexical frequency, word length and relationship type of the stimuli (matched)
span.quote: The criteria for all matches were lexical frequency (CELEX database; Baayen et al., 1993 ], word length, and relationship (part‐whole vs. functional

span.label: participant gender (restricted to males)
span.quote: To minimize the variance and increase homogeneity within our sample, only male subjects were measured.

span.label: session (modelled out of the fMRI analysis)
span.term: session (modelled out of the fMRI analysis)
span.quote: To avoid session‐specific effects we modeled the session effect in the fMRI data analysis.

span.label: 16 — number of participants scanned (all male)
span.quote: Sixteen healthy male subjects with an average age of 26.0 years (S.D. = 3.4) were recruited from the staff of the RWTH University Hospital Aachen and were paid a fee for participation.

span.label: 350 ms — stimulus onset asynchrony chosen to keep processing automatic rather than strategic
span.quote: According to Neely [ 1991 ] automatic processing occurs if the SOA is under 400 ms. Therefore, we used an SOA of 350 ms.

span.label: F (1, 15) = 14.73, P < 0.005 — main effect of relatedness on reaction time (the behavioural priming effect)
span.quote: The results of the ANOVA indicated that there was no main effect of modality ( F (1, 15) = 0.06, P = 0.81), but that subjects were faster in the related compared to the unrelated condition ( F (1, 15) = 14.73, P < 0.005).

span.quote: A further t ‐test of priming effect sizes in cross‐modal and unimodal conditions revealed that the picture–word priming effect did not differ from the word–word priming effect ( t (15) = −0.45, P = 0.66

span.label: 3.9% — proportion of reaction time trials removed as outliers before analysis
span.quote: Raw reaction time data were trimmed by eliminating responses exceeding the mean of every condition by more than two standard deviations to reduce skew [3.9%; Ratcliff, 1993 ].

span.label: 1 (= unrelated) to 7 (= highly‐related) — rating scale used in the norming pre-test to select strongly related word pairs
span.quote: Twelve volunteers not participating in the actual fMRI study were asked to rate word‐pair relations on a scale from 1 (= unrelated) to 7 (= highly‐related).
